parsed.title: Discussion on tax filing, domain purchase, and low‑profit web app ideas

topics.title: Complexity of tax filing and related costs

claims.text: The author paid about 1000 ₴ after re‑filing with the help of a contact, avoiding larger fines.
The inspector was described as corrupt and approved declarations without review.
The entire tax‑declaration procedure takes about an hour with Excel, at most a day per month.
Quarterly reports must be filed correctly.
Mistakes arise from mis‑matching columns and numbers in the calculation.
A calculator only works with hryvnia‑based FOP; otherwise transactions must be converted using the daily exchange rate.

topics.title: Domain purchase and need for a calculator

claims.text: Someone has not bought a domain yet.
A calculator (presumably for tax) is needed before money can be spent on a domain.
One participant doubts the domain will be bought.
The domain is considered a “silly thing” that won’t be useful.

topics.title: Viability of a low‑cost web app as a business

claims.text: Web platforms are the simplest but far less profitable than Android/iOS apps.
SEO for a web app is poor; even on the 10th Google page the site is not found.
There is no external traffic from social networks or contextual ads.
User retention is near zero because a paywall appears within the first 10 seconds.
Conversion is presumed zero; the product does not simplify anything or integrate with banks or tax cabinets.
A successful example uses a fast delivery (<1 week) and a cross‑platform stack (Flutter).
The discussed project (referred to as “spa”) is viewed skeptically and likely won’t sell.
LinkedIn audience size for such a product is shrinking, with technical/managerial posts dropping below 50%.

topics.title: Potential scam nature of the product and password access

claims.text: The app stores a single password locally as a 100% discount promo code.
Someone asks for the source code or password, implying it might be discoverable.
The reply suggests the asker never paid the 299 ₴ price.
Participants label the product as a “pirate” or “bandle” and mock the idea of paying for it.
One claims most LinkedIn users could hack the product easily.
The product is described as a “local‑first app” with USD/UAH rates updating every 5 minutes, but the paid part is just a bundle of code.
Another participant calls it a “free vibe‑code project” that’s nonsense and predicts nobody will buy it.

openQuestions.text: Is there a viable market of at least ten people willing to pay 299 ₴ for the described app?
What is the actual source code or password for the app, and can it be retrieved?
